context: Musashi warns against judgment captured by preference before the facts arrive. A partial heart does not merely favour; it distorts perception so that evidence is recruited to serve attachment. The line lands in loyalty, conflict, and self-assessment where fairness becomes expensive. It earned its place because bias is treated not as an intellectual flaw alone, but as a failure of discipline.

text_en: Throughout life, do not harbour greed.
text_original: 一生の間よくしん思はず。
translation_note: My faithful rendering from early modern Japanese.
context: Musashi treats greed as a standing orientation, not an isolated desire. The problem is not wanting a particular thing, but allowing acquisition to become the mind’s default answer to insufficiency. The line lands in work and ambition where every achievement immediately creates a larger hunger. It earned its place because it attacks the engine, not merely one excessive purchase.

text_en: Do not grieve at parting on any path.
text_original: いづれの道にもわかれをかなしまず。
translation_note: My faithful rendering from early modern Japanese.
context: Musashi refuses to let separation become an argument against having travelled together. Parting belongs to every path precisely because movement, change, and mortality belong to it. The line lands when grief demands that something valuable should therefore have been permanent. It earned its place because it offers no sentimental cure; it asks love to survive the end of possession.

text_en: Do not let the path of romantic attachment govern the heart.
text_original: れんぼの道思ひよるこゝろなし。
translation_note: My faithful rendering from early modern Japanese.
context: Musashi distinguishes feeling from rule. Attachment becomes dangerous when it is promoted from one force within life to the authority that decides identity, duty, and direction. The line lands in relationships where intensity is mistaken for truth and dependence for devotion. It earned its place because it does not flatter love by pretending love is incapable of conquest.

text_en: In all things, have no preferences.
text_original: 物毎にすきこのむ事なし。
translation_note: My faithful rendering from early modern Japanese.
context: Musashi attacks the small preferences that quietly become conditions for functioning. The aim is not sensory blankness but readiness: judgment should not collapse because circumstances are less pleasing than expected. The line lands when comfort, routine, or taste begins dictating what work can be done and where peace is permitted. It earned its place because dependence often enters wearing the harmless face of preference.

text_en: Have no desire for a private dwelling.
text_original: 私宅におゐてのぞむ心なし。
translation_note: My faithful rendering from early modern Japanese.
context: Musashi targets the wish to secure identity through a protected place of one’s own. A home can shelter life, but longing for possession can also narrow life around defence, status, and permanence. The line lands whenever safety becomes an expanding project that can never declare itself sufficient. It earned its place because it questions one of the most socially respectable forms of attachment.

text_en: Do not pursue fine food for yourself.
text_original: 身ひとつに美食をこのまず。
translation_note: My faithful rendering from early modern Japanese.
context: Musashi uses appetite as a training ground for independence. Pleasure is not condemned because it feels good; it becomes suspect when refinement turns into a requirement and ordinary nourishment into deprivation. The line lands in consumption habits that steadily raise the price of being content. It earned its place because discipline is tested most honestly where the stakes look too small to matter.

text_en: Do not seek goods or estates for your old age.
text_original: 老身に財宝所領もちゆる心なし。
translation_note: My faithful rendering from early modern Japanese.
context: Musashi confronts the fear that ageing can be made safe through accumulation alone. Preparation is practical, but possession becomes endless when it is asked to abolish vulnerability, dependence, and death. The line lands where prudent planning mutates into a life postponed for a security that never feels complete. It earned its place because it distinguishes provision from worship of protection.

text_en: You may abandon the body, but never abandon honour.
text_original: 身を捨ても名利はすてず。
translation_note: My faithful rendering from early modern Japanese; 名利 rendered here in its honour/reputation sense within the precept.
context: Musashi places a chosen standard above bodily preservation. The severity is deliberate: a life kept at the cost of everything that gave it direction may survive biologically while collapsing morally. The line lands when fear offers safety in exchange for silence, betrayal, or self-contempt. It earned its place because it names the value people praise until the moment it becomes expensive.

text_en: The ego is first and foremost a bodily ego.
text_original: Das Ich ist vor allem ein körperliches.
source_locator: Das Ich und das Es, Part II; GW XIII, p. 253
context: Freud refuses to treat the self as a clean intelligence merely housed in flesh. The ego grows from bodily sensation, boundary, vulnerability, and need. The line lands whenever someone tries to think their way out of exhaustion, desire, ageing, or shame as though the body were irrelevant evidence. It earned its place because it brings every grand theory of identity back to skin.

text_en: The dream is the guardian of sleep, not its disturber.
text_original: Der Traum ist der Hüter des Schlafes, nicht sein Störer.
context: Freud treats the dream as a compromise that lets sleep continue while pressure seeks expression. Its strange scenes are not random interruptions but disguised negotiations with what will not stay quiet. The line lands when anxiety appears irrational yet is performing a rough protective function beneath awareness. It earned its place because it turns disturbance into evidence of a mind trying to keep itself intact.

text_en: The unconscious is the true psychical reality.
text_original: Das Unbewußte ist das eigentlich reale Psychische.
context: Freud denies consciousness the right to call itself the whole mind. What feels most deliberate may sit above motives, memories, and conflicts that are no less real for being unseen. The line lands when a repeated choice contradicts the explanation a person gives for making it. It earned its place because it makes sincerity insufficient and self-knowledge an investigation.

text_en: The ego is the actual seat of anxiety.
text_original: Das Ich ist die eigentliche Angststätte.
source_locator: Hemmung, Symptom und Angst (1926), ch. VIII; GW XIV
context: Freud locates anxiety in the part of the mind forced to negotiate danger from instinct, conscience, and reality. Anxiety is therefore not merely weakness; it is the alarm of a divided authority under pressure. The line lands when competence on the outside hides a constant internal calculation of what may collapse. It earned its place because it makes fear structural before it makes it shameful.

text_en: Where they love, they do not desire; where they desire, they cannot love.
text_original: Wo sie lieben, begehren sie nicht, und wo sie begehren, können sie nicht lieben.
source_locator: “Über die allgemeinste Erniedrigung des Liebeslebens” (1912); GW VIII
context: Freud names a split in which tenderness and erotic desire are assigned to different people. The problem is not lack of feeling but an inability to let intimacy and appetite inhabit the same bond. The line lands in relationships that feel safe without being alive, or exciting without becoming close. It earned its place because it exposes a respectable division that quietly destroys both love and desire.

text_en: The uncanny is what leads back to something long known and once familiar.
text_original: Das Unheimliche ist jene Art des Schreckhaften, welche auf das Altbekannte, Längstvertraute zurückgeht.
source_locator: “Das Unheimliche” (1919), Part I; GW XII, p. 231
context: Freud makes the uncanny frightening precisely because it is not wholly foreign. Something familiar returns after repression has altered its face, and recognition arrives before explanation. The line lands when a place, person, or reaction feels disturbingly known without yielding a clear memory. It earned its place because it suggests that some fear is not warning us away, but calling us back.

text_en: The first requirement of civilization is justice.
text_original: Die erste Forderung der Kultur ist die Gerechtigkeit.
source_locator: Das Unbehagen in der Kultur, ch. III; GW XIV
context: Freud places justice at the point where private force is restrained by a rule applying beyond the strongest person. Civilization begins when power cannot rewrite the terms every time appetite changes. The line lands in institutions and families that praise harmony while protecting unequal permission. It earned its place because it strips culture of decoration and asks whom the rules actually bind.

text_en: Restriction in the possibility of enjoyment increases its preciousness.
text_original: Die Beschränkung in der Möglichkeit des Genusses erhöht dessen Kostbarkeit.
context: Freud argues that finitude can intensify value rather than cancel it. A pleasure does not become worthless because it ends; scarcity may be the condition that lets it matter. The line lands in grief and ageing, where anticipated loss tempts people to withdraw from what they still possess. It earned its place because it refuses to let impermanence become an alibi for emotional cowardice.

text_en: An intention is an impulse to action already approved, but postponed to a suitable moment.
text_original: Ein Vorsatz ist ein Impuls zur Handlung, der bereits Billigung gefunden hat, dessen Ausführung aber auf einen geeigneten Zeitpunkt verschoben wurde.
source_locator: Zur Psychopathologie des Alltagslebens, ch. VII, “Das Vergessen von Vorsätzen”; GW IV
context: Freud distinguishes wanting to act from having acted. An intention has passed internal approval, yet remains vulnerable to delay, resistance, and convenient forgetting. The line lands in work and relationships where sincerity is repeatedly offered in place of execution. It earned its place because it makes postponed goodness look less innocent than it sounds.

text_en: Individual freedom is not a cultural good.
text_original: Die individuelle Freiheit ist kein Kulturgut.
source_locator: Das Unbehagen in der Kultur, ch. III; GW XIV, p. 455
context: Freud states the conflict without pretending society and instinct naturally agree. Culture protects people by limiting what each person may do, then calls the limitation order. The line lands whenever security, belonging, and freedom are sold as though none requires sacrifice from the others. It earned its place because it denies the comforting fiction that every social good can be maximized at once.

text_en: The shadow is a moral problem that challenges the whole ego-personality.
text_original: Der Schatten ist ein moralisches Problem, welches das Ganze der Ichpersönlichkeit herausfordert.
translation_note: My faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung refuses to make the shadow a decorative symbol for hidden depth. It becomes a moral problem when disowned traits shape conduct while the conscious self claims innocence. The line lands whenever blame feels effortless and the same fault appears mysteriously in every opponent. It earned its place because it makes self-knowledge answerable for behaviour, not merely insight.

text_en: The persona is what one is not, but what oneself and others think one is.
text_original: Die Persona ist das, was man in Wirklichkeit nicht ist, aber was man selbst sowie andere glaubt, dass man ist.
translation_note: My faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung describes the persona as a negotiated public identity that can be mistaken for the person beneath it. The mask is useful until success inside it makes removal feel like annihilation. The line lands in careers and relationships where reputation is maintained long after it stops expressing a living self. It earned its place because it asks whether recognition is reaching you or only your role.

text_en: Individuation means becoming an individual—and becoming one’s own self.
text_original: Individuation bedeutet: zum Einzelwesen werden, und, insofern wir unter Individualität unsere innerste, letzte und unvergleichbare Einzigartigkeit verstehen, zum eigenen Selbst werden.
source_locator: “The Relations between the Ego and the Unconscious,” CW 7, §266
translation_note: Condensed faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung defines growth as differentiation, not improved conformity. Becoming oneself requires separating an inner direction from collective expectation without pretending one can live outside relationship. The line lands when a socially successful life begins to feel strangely uninhabited. It earned its place because it makes belonging without selfhood look like a sophisticated disappearance.

text_en: Man needs difficulties; they are necessary for health.
text_original: Der Mensch bedarf der Schwierigkeiten, sie gehören zu seiner Gesundheit.
translation_note: My faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung treats difficulty as part of psychic development rather than a defect in the plan. Resistance forces capacities and conflicts into view that comfort can leave untested. The line lands when a frictionless life is mistaken for a healthy one and every obstacle is pathologized. It earned its place because it does not console the reader by promising ease.

text_en: Neurosis is always a substitute for legitimate suffering.
text_original: Die Neurose ist immer ein Ersatz für legitimes Leiden.
translation_note: My faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung suggests that symptoms can grow around pain a person refuses to suffer directly. Avoidance does not remove the wound; it may replace a finite grief with a larger, less intelligible captivity. The line lands when endless analysis protects someone from mourning, choosing, or admitting what cannot be repaired. It earned its place because it asks whether the cure being sought is actually permission not to hurt.

text_en: The least thing with meaning is worth more in life than the greatest without it.
text_original: Das Geringste mit Sinn ist im Leben mehr wert als das Größte ohne Sinn.
translation_note: My faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung refuses to let scale substitute for significance. Achievement becomes psychologically empty when its size is the only answer to why it matters. The line lands in work built around expansion, visibility, and accumulation after purpose has quietly left the room. It earned its place because it can make a grand success look smaller than one honest act.

text_en: Everything psychic is pregnant with the future.
text_original: Alles Psychische ist schwanger mit Zukunft.
translation_note: My faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung sees the psyche as carrying tendencies that have not yet taken conscious form. A mood, dream, or conflict may be less a residue than an early movement toward what is coming. The line lands when present confusion is judged only by what caused it and not by what it is trying to become. It earned its place because it gives uncertainty direction without pretending to predict the destination.

text_en: The dream is a theatre in which the dreamer is scene, player, author, public, and critic.
text_original: Der Traum ist jenes Theater, wo der Träumer Szene, Spieler, Souffleur, Regisseur, Autor, Publikum und Kritiker ist.
translation_note: Condensed faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung makes every figure in the dream part of one psychic event. The enemy, witness, stage, and verdict may all express positions the waking self has separated. The line lands when a dream is treated as a message about everyone except the dreamer. It earned its place because it removes the safest seat in the theatre: innocent spectator.

text_en: As fear once stood in the way of life, so now it stands in the way of death.
text_original: Wie früher die Furcht als Hemmnis vor dem Leben stand, so steht sie jetzt vor dem Tode.
translation_note: My faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung describes fear as capable of obstructing opposite tasks at different stages. Earlier it may prevent full living; later it may prevent the surrender that mortality demands. The line lands in ageing and grief when control continues fighting a transition it cannot reverse. It earned its place because it asks whether the same defence that once protected life is now narrowing it.

text_en: Natural life is the nourishing soil of the soul.
text_original: Der Nährboden der Seele ist das natürliche Leben.
translation_note: My faithful rendering from German; the standard Hull translation is copyrighted.
context: Jung warns against a spirituality or psychology severed from ordinary life. The soul is fed through body, work, season, relationship, and the limits of being an animal among others. The line lands when reflection becomes an elegant escape from sleep, movement, duty, and contact. It earned its place because it makes transcendence answer to the ground beneath it.

text_en: If the body is not a thing, it is a situation.
text_original: Si le corps n’est pas une chose, il est une situation.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Première partie, ch. I, “Les données de la biologie”
translation_note: My faithful rendering from French; the conditional “Si” is retained.
context: Beauvoir refuses to reduce the body either to destiny or to inert material. A body is lived through possibilities, restrictions, tools, norms, and the world it can reach. The line lands whenever biology is used to close a question that social conditions are still actively shaping. It earned its place because it turns the body from a verdict into contested ground.

text_en: Humanity is male, and man defines woman not in herself but relative to him.
text_original: L’humanité est mâle et l’homme définit la femme non en soi mais relativement à lui.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Introduction
translation_note: My faithful rendering from French; the original retains its gendered wording.
context: Beauvoir identifies the power hidden in who gets to appear universal. Man becomes the unmarked human standard while woman is described as variation, relation, and exception. The line lands wherever one group’s experience is called neutral and everyone else must explain their difference. It earned its place because it exposes domination operating through grammar before policy.

text_en: No group defines itself as One without immediately setting up the Other opposite itself.
text_original: Aucune collectivité ne se définit jamais comme Une sans immédiatement poser l’Autre en face de soi.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Introduction
context: Beauvoir shows identity being built through opposition. A group secures its unity by naming someone outside it as strange, lesser, or threatening. The line lands in workplaces, families, and politics when belonging suddenly requires a convenient enemy. It earned its place because it makes solidarity suspicious at the exact moment it feels most righteous.

text_en: True otherness belongs to a consciousness separate from mine and identical to it.
text_original: La véritable altérité est celle d’une conscience séparée de la mienne et identique à elle.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Troisième partie, ch. I
context: Beauvoir defines the other person as both irreducibly separate and equally a subject. Relationship fails when difference is erased, but it also fails when equality is denied. The line lands in love and leadership where understanding becomes a polite name for absorption or control. It earned its place because it demands closeness without possession.

text_en: Human life is never fullness and rest; it is lack, movement, and struggle.
text_original: La vie de l’homme n’est jamais plénitude et repos, elle est manque et mouvement, elle est lutte.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Troisième partie, ch. I
context: Beauvoir rejects the fantasy that a completed life would finally become still. Human existence keeps opening distance between what is and what is pursued. The line lands when rest is expected to cure every dissatisfaction and movement itself is mistaken for failure. It earned its place because it offers no final sofa on which the self can stop becoming.

text_en: Possession is a way of seeking being.
text_original: La possession est un mode de recherche de l’être.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Troisième partie, ch. I
context: Beauvoir sees possession as an attempt to secure identity through what can be held. The object, status, or person becomes a defence against the instability of existing without guarantees. The line lands when acquisition promises not merely pleasure but proof that one finally is someone. It earned its place because it makes ownership confess the fear beneath it.

text_en: To change the face of the world, one must first be firmly anchored in it.
text_original: Pour changer la face du monde, il faut y être d’abord solidement ancré.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Deuxième partie, ch. V
context: Beauvoir ties transformation to concrete position and agency. Moral vision without access, competence, or material footing risks remaining a beautiful protest made from the margins. The line lands in work and public life when ambition for impact outruns the structures needed to carry it. It earned its place because it forces idealism to acquire weight.

text_en: Temptation too is an obstacle, and even one of the most dangerous.
text_original: On n’a pas assez compris que la tentation aussi est un obstacle, et même un des plus dangereux.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Deuxième partie, ch. V
context: Beauvoir notices that oppression does not rely only on prohibition. It can offer comfort, prestige, or dependence attractive enough to make surrender feel freely chosen. The line lands when the easier path rewards a person for abandoning the independence they claim to want. It earned its place because it reveals the cage with cushions as the more dangerous design.

text_en: An existing being is nothing other than what it does.
text_original: Un existant n’est rien d’autre que ce qu’il fait.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome I, Troisième partie, ch. III
context: Beauvoir denies a secret essence that excuses a life from its actions. Possibility matters only when conduct gives it form in the world. The line lands whenever talent, intention, or identity is used to claim credit for work never undertaken. It earned its place because it removes the flattering distance between who you say you are and what you repeatedly do.

text_en: Every oppression creates a state of war.
text_original: Toute oppression crée un état de guerre.
source_locator: Le Deuxième Sexe, Tome II, Conclusion
context: Beauvoir rejects the idea that domination produces stable peace. Silence under inequality is already conflict, even when one side has been denied the means to answer openly. The line lands in relationships and institutions that call obedience harmony and resistance the first act of aggression. It earned its place because it names the war before the oppressed are blamed for revealing it.

text_en: Nothing is more difficult, doubtful, or dangerous than introducing a new order.
text_original: Non è cosa più difficile a trattare, né più dubia a riuscire, né più pericolosa a maneggiare, che farsi capo ad introdurre nuovi ordini.
context: Machiavelli treats change as a conflict of interests, not a presentation problem. The old order has beneficiaries ready to fight, while future beneficiaries are uncertain and cautious. The line lands in transformation programs where applause is mistaken for commitment and resistance is dismissed as misunderstanding. It earned its place because it makes innovation answer to power, not enthusiasm.

text_en: It is easy to persuade people of something, but difficult to keep them persuaded.
text_original: È facile a persuadere loro una cosa, ma è difficile fermargli in quella persuasione.
context: Machiavelli separates the moment of conviction from the durability of belief. People may accept a new idea before habit, fear, and changing advantage test whether it can hold. The line lands in leadership and relationships where one strong conversation is treated as permanent alignment. It earned its place because it asks what remains after persuasion loses the room.

text_en: Men offend either from fear or from hatred.
text_original: Gli uomini offendono o per paura, o per odio.
context: Machiavelli reduces aggression to two forces that leaders often underestimate. Fear can strike pre-emptively, while hatred waits for an opening to repay injury. The line lands when another person’s hostility is treated as irrational instead of examined for the threat or resentment beneath it. It earned its place because it makes danger legible without making it noble.

text_en: Injuries should be done all at once; benefits should be given little by little.
text_original: Le ingiurie si debbono fare tutte insieme; li beneficii si debbono fare a poco a poco.
context: Machiavelli is describing how power manages memory, shock, and gratitude. Concentrated harm fades from immediate sensation, while repeated benefits renew dependence and recognition. The line lands in politics and management because institutions still choreograph pain and reward over time. It earned its place because its cold efficiency exposes manipulation more clearly than moral language does.

text_en: Good laws and good arms are the chief foundations of every state.
text_original: I principali fondamenti che abbino tutti li stati sono le buone legge e le buone arme.
context: Machiavelli joins legitimacy to capacity. Rules without force may become wishes, while force without rules becomes predation. The line lands in organizations where elegant governance is announced without the means to enforce it, or enforcement operates without credible standards. It earned its place because it refuses to let principle and power pretend they can survive apart.

text_en: A man who professes goodness everywhere must be ruined among so many who are not good.
text_original: Un uomo che voglia fare in tutte le parti professione di buono, conviene che rovini fra tanti che non sono buoni.
context: Machiavelli warns that virtue performed without regard to circumstance can become self-destruction. The claim is not that goodness is foolish, but that moral identity alone does not neutralize predatory conditions. The line lands when decency is confused with having no boundaries, leverage, or answer to bad faith. It earned its place because it attacks the vanity that sometimes hides inside being harmless.

text_en: Nothing consumes itself so much as liberality.
text_original: Non ci è cosa che consumi sé stessa quanto la liberalità.
context: Machiavelli argues that generosity can destroy the resources required to sustain its reputation. Giving becomes politically unstable when it demands extraction, debt, or later cruelty to continue. The line lands in leadership and personal life where visible generosity is financed by invisible depletion. It earned its place because it asks who eventually pays for the virtue everyone applauds.

text_en: A deceiver will always find someone who lets himself be deceived.
text_original: Colui che inganna troverà sempre chi si lascerà ingannare.
context: Machiavelli places deception in a relationship between appetite and manipulation. The lie succeeds not only because someone invents it, but because someone needs its promise badly enough to suspend scrutiny. The line lands in work and love when flattering explanations survive evidence that would destroy less convenient stories. It earned its place because it gives the deceived an uncomfortable share of the scene.

text_en: Prudence consists in knowing difficulties and choosing the least bad as good.
text_original: La prudenza consiste in saper cognoscere la qualità degli inconvenienti, e prendere il manco tristo per buono.
context: Machiavelli defines prudence inside imperfect choices, not ideal solutions. Mature judgment may consist in recognizing which damage can be carried when every option contains loss. The line lands in executive and personal dilemmas where waiting for a clean answer becomes another costly decision. It earned its place because it makes wisdom look less pure and more responsible.

text_en: A prince who relies entirely on fortune is ruined when she changes.
text_original: Quel Principe che si appoggia tutto in sulla fortuna, rovina come quella varia.
context: Machiavelli distinguishes success from control over the conditions producing it. Fortune can reward a method long enough to make adaptability feel unnecessary, then expose dependence when circumstances turn. The line lands in careers and businesses that mistake a favourable environment for permanent competence. It earned its place because it asks how much of confidence is merely weather.

text_en: It was merely the name men gave to their mistakes.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. IV
translation_note: Exact standalone sentence from the English original.
context: Wilde punctures the dignity people award to repetition after the damage is done. Calling something experience can turn failure into status without proving that anything was learned. The line lands when age or tenure is used to silence scrutiny of the same old mistake. It earned its place because one polished word loses its alibi in a single sentence.

text_en: There is only one thing worse than being talked about, and that is not being talked about.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. I
context: Wilde exposes reputation as an appetite that can prefer scandal to invisibility. Attention wounds, but absence threatens the ego with a more complete kind of disappearance. The line lands in work and social life when outrage becomes acceptable collateral for remaining central. It earned its place because it makes vanity confess that criticism may still feel like nourishment.

text_en: A man cannot be too careful in the choice of his enemies.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. I
context: Wilde treats enemies as part of the identity one stages before the world. Opposition can flatter, elevate, or expose a person as efficiently as friendship. The line lands when conflict is cultivated because the right antagonist makes one look more important or principled. It earned its place because it turns hostility into a form of self-curation.

text_en: The books that the world calls immoral are books that show the world its own shame.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. XIX
context: Wilde suggests that moral outrage may be displaced recognition. A work becomes intolerable not because it invents corruption, but because it reflects what respectable society prefers to keep unowned. The line lands whenever exposure is condemned more fiercely than the reality exposed. It earned its place because it asks whether offence is conscience speaking or shame defending itself.

text_en: Conscience and cowardice are really the same things.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. I
context: Wilde gives a dangerous character the elegant lie that restraint is only fear wearing moral clothes. The sentence matters because seduction often works by redescribing conscience as weakness. It lands before a betrayal or reckless choice when hesitation is mocked as lack of courage. It earned its place because the line is persuasive enough to require resistance, not applause.

text_en: Nothing can cure the soul but the senses, just as nothing can cure the senses but the soul.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. II
context: Wilde binds body and inner life into a reciprocal medicine. Pure sensation can interrupt abstraction, while meaning can rescue sensation from becoming mere appetite. The line lands when a person tries to heal through thought alone or through stimulation alone. It earned its place because it denies both the ascetic and the hedonist a complete answer.

text_en: There are only two tragedies: not getting what one wants, and getting it.
text_original: There are only two tragedies in life: one is not getting what one wants, and the other is getting it.
context: Wilde makes desire dangerous in both defeat and success. Failure preserves the fantasy that fulfilment would have completed us, while success can reveal that the fantasy was carrying more meaning than the object. The line lands after promotions, conquests, and relationships that arrive without producing the promised self. It earned its place because it leaves desire nowhere comfortable to hide.

text_en: The aim of life is self-development.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. II
context: Wilde’s speaker makes self-development sound like the highest duty, but the novel tests how quickly that ideal can become permission for appetite. Growth without judgment may merely enlarge whatever already rules us. The line lands in cultures where every indulgence can be marketed as authenticity. It earned its place because its beauty is inseparable from the danger of believing it too easily.

text_en: To define is to limit.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. XVII
context: Wilde compresses the violence and usefulness of definition into four words. A definition clarifies by excluding, and every clean boundary leaves something living outside it. The line lands in relationships and identity when a label begins as understanding and ends as a cage. It earned its place because it makes precision answer for what it cuts away.

text_en: Whenever a man does a thoroughly stupid thing, it is always from the noblest motives.
source_locator: The Picture of Dorian Gray, ch. VI
context: Wilde mocks the moral decoration people place around reckless choices. Noble motives can protect stupidity from examination because questioning the decision begins to look like questioning virtue itself. The line lands in work and love when good intentions demand immunity from consequences. It earned its place because it makes righteousness sound like the most expensive form of carelessness.

text_en: Nothing was your own except the few cubic centimetres inside your skull.
source_locator: Nineteen Eighty-Four, Part I, ch. II
context: Orwell reduces private freedom to the last interior space power has not yet occupied. The sentence is not triumphant; even that refuge is under surveillance and pressure. It lands whenever external conformity demands not only obedience but genuine inward agreement. It earned its place because it shows how little freedom may remain before surrender becomes total.

text_en: If you want to keep a secret, you must also hide it from yourself.
source_locator: Nineteen Eighty-Four, Part III, ch. IV
context: Orwell shows repression becoming the final technology of secrecy. Under sufficient danger, survival may require a person to destroy conscious access to what they know. The line lands in families, institutions, and private guilt where denial is maintained not for others but for the self. It earned its place because it makes self-deception look like both defence and defeat.

text_en: Perhaps one did not want to be loved so much as to be understood.
source_locator: Nineteen Eighty-Four, Part II, ch. VII
context: Orwell separates affection from recognition. Love can comfort while leaving the central experience of another person unseen or misread. The line lands in relationships where reassurance is abundant but honest comprehension remains absent. It earned its place because it names the loneliness that can survive inside being loved.

text_en: Sanity is not statistical.
source_locator: Nineteen Eighty-Four, Part I, ch. VII
context: Orwell denies the majority the power to manufacture truth by counting itself. A belief can be universal and still be false, while one isolated mind can remain sane against the crowd. The line lands when consensus is offered as a substitute for evidence or conscience. It earned its place because it gives solitude intellectual dignity without making it comfortable.

text_en: Orthodoxy means not thinking—not needing to think. Orthodoxy is unconsciousness.
source_locator: Nineteen Eighty-Four, Part I, ch. V
context: Orwell defines successful orthodoxy as the elimination of mental effort, not merely the enforcement of correct answers. The strongest system makes forbidden conclusions impossible to formulate. The line lands wherever approved language arrives preassembled and doubt feels like a failure of belonging. It earned its place because it identifies obedience at the point where the guard is no longer needed.

text_en: Until they become conscious they will never rebel, and until after they have rebelled they cannot become conscious.
source_locator: Nineteen Eighty-Four, Part I, ch. VII
translation_note: Exact excerpt from the English original.
context: Orwell traps political awakening inside a circular dependency. People need awareness to act, yet action may be what finally produces awareness. The line lands in personal and collective situations where waiting to feel ready preserves the very condition that prevents readiness. It earned its place because it turns the first act of freedom into a leap without prior permission.

text_en: Power is in tearing human minds to pieces and putting them together again in new shapes of your own choosing.
source_locator: Nineteen Eighty-Four, Part III, ch. III
translation_note: Exact excerpt from the English original.
context: Orwell defines domination as authorship over another person’s reality. Control is complete when the victim’s mind is broken and rebuilt to reproduce the ruler’s categories. The line lands wherever power seeks not compliance but confession, gratitude, or belief. It earned its place because it shows that the final territory of tyranny is the meaning a person gives their own pain.

text_en: Political language is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable.
source_locator: “Politics and the English Language,” concluding paragraph
translation_note: Short excerpt from the English original.
context: Orwell treats corrupted language as operational equipment for corrupted action. Euphemism does not merely conceal brutality; it makes brutality administratively and morally easier to perform. The line lands whenever bloodless wording removes agents, victims, and consequences from a decision. It earned its place because it makes bad prose look dangerous rather than merely ugly.

text_en: The opinion that art should have nothing to do with politics is itself a political attitude.
source_locator: “Why I Write,” discussion of political purpose
context: Orwell denies neutrality to the refusal of politics. Choosing not to name power still leaves existing arrangements untouched and therefore takes a side in practice. The line lands when withdrawal is presented as purity rather than a position with beneficiaries. It earned its place because it removes the moral shelter of being above the conflict.

text_en: The essence of being human is that one does not seek perfection.
translation_note: Short excerpt from the English original.
context: Orwell distrusts moral perfection when it requires the removal of attachment, partiality, pleasure, and ordinary contradiction. Humanity appears in compromised loyalties and finite loves, not in antiseptic consistency. The line lands when virtue demands becoming less alive in order to become less blameworthy. It earned its place because it makes flawless goodness answer for the human costs it refuses to touch.
